In dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during a spatial working memory task, persistent firing of Delay cells was abolished by local blockade of NR2B-containing NMDA receptors or by systemic ketamine, while AMPA receptors contributed background depolarization; many Response cells were instead sensitive to AMPA receptor blockade and increased firing after ketamine (monkey).

Stimulating alpha2A adrenoceptors, inhibiting cAMP or blocking HCN channels enhanced the spatially tuned delay-related firing of prefrontal neurons, whereas excessive cAMP collapsed it; HCN channels and alpha2A adrenoceptors were colocalized in dendritic spines, and blocking or knocking down HCN1 channels in prefrontal cortex improved working memory (monkeys and rats).

Review: even mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities, and more prolonged stress causes architectural changes in prefrontal dendrites; the signalling pathways involved offer clues to why insults that disinhibit stress signalling can lead to symptoms of prefrontal dysfunction in mental illness.

In 175 patients with schizophrenia, 219 unaffected siblings and 55 controls, the low-activity Met allele of the COMT Val108/158 Met polymorphism predicted fewer perseverative errors on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test and a more efficient prefrontal response during working memory, and the Val allele was transmitted more often to offspring with schizophrenia. The authors suggest that the Val allele, by increasing prefrontal dopamine catabolism, impairs prefrontal cognition and slightly increases risk for schizophrenia (human).

Review: proposes that cognitive control stems from the active maintenance of patterns of activity in prefrontal cortex that represent goals and the means to achieve them, which provide bias signals guiding the flow of activity in other brain structures along the pathways a task needs.

In monkeys performing an object sequence memory task, prefrontal neurons with mixed selectivity encoded distributed information about all task-relevant aspects, giving high-dimensional representations with a computational advantage for readout; this dimensionality collapsed in error trials (monkey).

In monkeys trained to flexibly select and integrate noisy sensory inputs towards a choice, the complex responses of single prefrontal neurons were understood as part of population dynamics that a trained recurrent neural network reproduced, suggesting that selection and integration are two aspects of a single dynamical process within the same prefrontal circuits (monkey).

In prefrontal cortex during a working memory task, brief bursts of narrow-band gamma (45-100 Hz) accompanied encoding and re-activation of sensory information, while beta (20-35 Hz) bursts reflected a default state interrupted by encoding and decoding; this supports the hypothesis that working memory is manifested by discrete oscillatory dynamics and spiking, not sustained activity (monkey).

Monkeys learned two abstract rules (judge whether two successive pictures were the same or different, depending on which rule was in effect) and applied them to new pictures; the most prevalent neuronal activity in prefrontal cortex reflected the coding of these abstract rules (monkey).

During economic choice between goods, neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex encoded the value of offered and chosen goods independently of visuospatial factors and motor responses, so OFC neurons seem to be a good candidate network for the value assignment underlying economic choice (monkey).

Theory: proposes that the orbitofrontal cortex provides a labeling of the current task state, a cognitive map of task space used for reinforcement learning elsewhere in the brain, which is especially critical when task states include unobservable information; the framework is used to explain findings in reversal learning, delayed alternation, extinction and devaluation.

Excitotoxic, fiber-sparing lesions confined to the orbitofrontal cortex altered neither object reversal learning nor fear of snakes, and a previously reported loss of inhibitory control was traced to damage to nearby fiber tracts; the authors conclude that OFC has a more specialized role in reward-guided behavior and emotion than thought, including value updating (monkey).

Monkeys with bilateral orbital prefrontal removals showed attenuated reinforcer devaluation effects and were impaired on object reversal learning, but learned object discriminations and chose among foods normally, suggesting that orbital prefrontal cortex is critical for response selection based on predicted reward outcomes (monkey).

In the Stroop colour-naming task, controlling for repetition effects, conflict-related activity in the anterior cingulate cortex predicted both greater prefrontal cortex activity and adjustments in behaviour, supporting a role of ACC conflict monitoring in engaging cognitive control (human).

Humans alternated between comparative decision-making and foraging, which depended on distinct mechanisms in ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex: vmPFC encoded the values of specific well-defined options, whereas ACC encoded the average value of the foraging environment and the cost of foraging (human).

Theory: proposes that the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex allocates cognitive control according to its expected value, integrating the expected payoff of a controlled process, the amount of control it needs and the cost of cognitive effort to decide whether, where and how much control to allocate.

Infralimbic neurons fired to the tone only when rats were recalling extinction on the day after extinction training, and the rats that froze least showed the greatest increase in these responses; pairing conditioned tones with brief infralimbic stimulation lowered freezing in rats that had not been extinguished. The authors suggest that consolidation of extinction potentiates infralimbic activity, which inhibits fear (rat).

Inactivation with muscimol before extinction training showed dissociable roles: inactivating infralimbic cortex spared fear expression but impaired the acquisition and memory of extinction, inactivating prelimbic cortex impaired fear expression without affecting extinction memory, and inactivating the basolateral amygdala or ventral hippocampus impaired both (rat).

Prelimbic neurons showed sustained conditioned responses to a 30 s tone that correlated second by second with freezing, and their persistence after extinction training was associated with failure to express extinction memory; the authors suggest that prelimbic cortex transforms transient amygdala inputs into a sustained output that drives conditioned fear (rat).

Theta-range (4-12 Hz) synchrony between medial prefrontal cortex and basolateral amygdala increased only in mice that differentiated aversive from safe cues, and during recognized safety, in both learned fear and innate anxiety, BLA firing became entrained to theta input from mPFC, suggesting a safety-signalling mechanism by which mPFC diminishes fear (mouse).

Rats with prelimbic lesions were insensitive to changes in reward value after either limited or extended training, whereas rats with infralimbic lesions stayed sensitive to goal value even after extended training; this double dissociation suggests that prelimbic cortex supports goal-directed performance and infralimbic cortex lets extended training override it as habits form (rat).

Inhibiting parvalbumin interneurons optogenetically suppressed gamma oscillations in vivo, whereas driving them was sufficient to generate emergent gamma-frequency rhythmicity; gamma-frequency modulation of excitatory input enhanced signal transmission in neocortex by reducing circuit noise and amplifying circuit signals (mouse).

Optogenetically inhibiting somatostatin, but not parvalbumin, interneurons in medial prefrontal cortex during the encoding phase of a spatial working memory task impaired accuracy, with decreased hippocampal-prefrontal synchrony and impaired spatial encoding by mPFC neurons, suggesting that interneuron dysfunction may contribute to cognitive deficits in schizophrenia (mouse).

Direct hippocampal-prefrontal afferents were critical for encoding, but not maintenance or retrieval, of spatial cues in a working memory task; prefrontal units represented the cues in a hippocampal-input-dependent manner only during cue encoding, and successful encoding appeared to be mediated by gamma-frequency synchrony between the two structures (mouse).

Simultaneous tetrode recordings from hippocampal CA1 and medial prefrontal cortex showed that correlated firing between the two was selectively enhanced during behaviour that recruits spatial working memory, paralleled by enhanced coupling in the 4-12 Hz theta range (rat).

In mice using two rules to guide attention, mediodorsal thalamic input sustained rule representations in prefrontal cortex without relaying categorical information, by amplifying local PFC connectivity so that rule-specific neural sequences emerge; broadly enhancing PFC excitability diminished rule specificity and performance, whereas enhancing mediodorsal excitability improved both (mouse).

Pathway-specific inhibition showed directional interactions: mediodorsal thalamus-to-mPFC projections supported working memory maintenance and mPFC-to-MD projections supported the subsequent choice; mPFC neurons with elevated delay spiking, absent on error trials, required MD input for sustained maintenance, and enhancing MD excitability improved performance (mouse).

Many medial prefrontal neurons were modulated moment to moment by rats' decision to act in a challenging situation, yet activating mPFC principal neurons as a whole had no detectable effect; selectively activating mPFC cells projecting to the dorsal raphe nucleus induced a profound, rapid and reversible effect on selection of the active behavioural state (rat).

Dominance rank in mice was transitive and relatively stable; layer V pyramidal neurons of medial prefrontal cortex received stronger excitatory synaptic inputs in higher-ranking mice, and molecular manipulations that increased or decreased synaptic efficacy in dorsal mPFC neurons moved animals up or down the social rank (mouse).

Simultaneous recordings showed that prefrontal neurons reflected the target location first during top-down attention, whereas posterior parietal neurons signalled it earlier during bottom-up attention; frontal-parietal synchrony was stronger at lower frequencies during top-down and at higher frequencies during bottom-up attention (monkey).

Damage to lateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann's area 9) caused a loss of inhibitory control in attentional selection, whereas damage to orbitofrontal cortex caused a loss of inhibitory control in affective processing, impairing the ability to alter behaviour when the emotional significance of stimuli changed (marmoset).

Ibotenic acid lesions of medial frontal cortex impaired neither initial acquisition nor reversal learning but selectively impaired shifting of attentional set, as in primates with prefrontal lesions; the authors conclude that rat medial frontal cortex has functional similarity to primate lateral prefrontal cortex (rat).

In 20 medication-free patients with chronic schizophrenia and 25 controls, blood flow to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex rose during the Wisconsin Card Sort in controls but not in patients, a regionally specific difference; in patients, DLPFC blood flow correlated positively with card-sort performance (human).

Dendritic spine density on deep layer 3 pyramidal neurons of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (area 46) was 23% lower in 15 subjects with schizophrenia than in normal controls, whereas superficial layer 3 neurons of area 46 and layer 3 neurons of primary visual cortex did not differ significantly: a region- and disease-specific decrease (human).

Review: convergent findings indicate that deficient TrkB signalling reduces GABA synthesis in parvalbumin-containing interneurons of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in schizophrenia, and the resulting alteration in perisomatic inhibition of pyramidal neurons contributes to a diminished capacity for the gamma-frequency synchronized activity required for working memory.

Chronic deep brain stimulation of white matter tracts adjacent to the subgenual cingulate gyrus (Brodmann area 25), a region metabolically overactive in treatment-resistant depression, was associated with striking and sustained remission in four of six patients, with reduced local blood flow and changes in downstream limbic and cortical sites (human).

Ketamine rapidly activated the mTOR pathway, increasing synaptic signalling proteins and the number and function of new spine synapses in prefrontal cortex; blocking mTOR signalling completely blocked ketamine's induction of synaptogenesis and its behavioural responses in models of depression (rat).

Longitudinal imaging of medial prefrontal microcircuits showed that depression-related behaviour was associated with branch-specific elimination of dendritic spines on prefrontal projection neurons; antidepressant-dose ketamine selectively rescued eliminated spines and restored coordinated ensemble activity, and this spinogenesis was required for long-term maintenance, but not initial induction, of ketamine's effects on motivated escape behaviour (mouse).

In 824 MRI scans from 223 children with ADHD and 223 typically developing controls, the age of peak cortical thickness was delayed in ADHD throughout most of the cerebrum (median 10.5 versus 7.5 years), most prominently in prefrontal regions important for control of cognitive processes including attention and motor planning (human).

Damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex causes a defect in real-life decision-making; on a new task simulating such decisions under uncertainty, with reward and punishment, prefrontal patients, unlike controls, were oblivious to the future consequences of their actions and seemed guided by immediate prospects only (human).

Six patients with focal bilateral damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex gave abnormally 'utilitarian' judgements on moral dilemmas that pit aggregate welfare against highly emotionally aversive actions, but normal judgements on other classes of dilemmas, indicating that for this selective set the VMPC is critical for normal judgements of right and wrong (human).

Review: a meta-analysis found dramatic differences in the focus of human and rodent PFC research, leading rodent atlases use inconsistent anatomical terms and criteria for PFC areas, and a survey of PFC researchers found little consensus; the authors propose an alternative scheme for interpreting rodent data based on the corpus callosum and primate anterior cingulate nomenclature.

A type of midbrain dopamine neuron with unconventional fast-firing properties and small DAT/TH mRNA ratios projects selectively to prefrontal cortex, the nucleus accumbens core and medial shell and the basolateral amygdala, whereas conventional slow-firing dopamine neurons project only to the lateral accumbens shell and dorsolateral striatum; only the mesoprefrontal neurons lack functional somatodendritic Girk2-coupled D2 autoreceptors (mouse).

Locus coeruleus cells innervating different cortical regions were biochemically and electrophysiologically distinct, eliciting greater release of norepinephrine in prefrontal than in motor cortex, which challenges the view of the LC as a relatively homogeneous modulator of forebrain activity (rat).

Optogenetically evoked dopamine release from VTA projections in medial prefrontal cortex was neither rewarding nor aversive, but repeatedly pairing it with an auditory stimulus sped later learning to discriminate that stimulus, with appetitive or aversive outcomes alike; the pairings increased mPFC responses to the stimulus, and D1 or D2 antagonists in mPFC impaired discrimination. The authors conclude that dopamine transients tune mPFC neurons for recognizing behaviourally relevant events during learning (mouse).

WGA-HRP injections into the mediodorsal nucleus labeled cells and terminals in prefrontal cortex in a nucleus-to-field pattern: the magnocellular part with ventral and medial prefrontal areas (11-14), the parvicellular part with dorsolateral and dorsomedial areas (46, 9 and 8B); MD terminals were confined to layer IV and adjacent deep layer III (monkey).

Retrograde tracing in 27 monkeys showed that most hippocampal-formation neurons projecting to prefrontal cortex target medial areas, followed by orbital areas, whereas lateral prefrontal areas receive only a few, mostly subicular, neurons and their most robust input from the presubiculum and area 29a-c (monkey).

Tracers injected in the amygdala showed that prefrontal areas vary vastly in their connections with it, densest in posterior orbitofrontal and posterior medial cortices and sparsest in anterior lateral areas, especially area 10; cingulate areas 25 and 24 sent comparatively more projections to the amygdala than they received, whereas caudal orbitofrontal areas were more receivers than senders (monkey).
